chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Zurara from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him)
Regarding a man who ordered another man to kill a man, and he killed him, it was said: The one who killed him is executed for him, and the commander is imprisoned until he dies.

As for what Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ibn Mahbub from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding a man who ordered his slave to kill a man, and he killed him, it was said: The master is executed for him.

And Ali from his father from al-Nufali from al-Sakuni from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said regarding a man who ordered his slave to kill a man, and he killed him: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: Is the man's slave not like his sword? The master is executed and the slave is entrusted to prison.

The resolution in these two narrations is to interpret them as referring to one who is accustomed to ordering his slaves to kill people, forcing them into it and compelling them to do so. Indeed, one whose image is this is obligated to be executed because he is a corrupter on earth.
And we said that because the first narration is consistent with the apparent meaning of the Quran. Allah, the Exalted, said: 'For a life, a life.'
And we know that he meant the killing soul, not others, without dispute.
Therefore, that which contradicts that should not be acted upon.

key_terms.بِالنَّفْسِ بِالنَّفْسِ: For a life, a life (Quranic verse)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference in execution ruling between a free man and a slave when ordered to kill?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi resolves the apparent contradiction between the two reports by distinguishing between a commander who merely orders a killing and one who habitually compels his slave, treating the latter as a 'mufsid fi al-ard' (corrupter on earth) liable for execution. This interpretation aligns the hadith with the Quranic principle of 'a life for a life' (2:178), clarifying that the death penalty applies specifically to the killer, while the commander's imprisonment serves as a preventive measure unless his compulsion is habitual and coercive. The narration further links back to Imam Ali’s (AS) judicial reasoning, emphasizing the master's slave as an extension of his will ('like his sword').
